newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to speed up state bank privatisation - PM.
newsitem.headline: Romania to speed up state bank privatisation - PM.

text.p: Romania's Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said on Friday that his government planned to speed the selloff of state banks, as part of broad reforms agreed with international lenders.
"The pace of privatisation must be accelerated in all sectors, including banking," Ciorbea told a meeting of leaders of his centrist ruling National Peasant Party.

"We must adopt a package of bills which will allow foreign investors to get equity in Romanian banks," he said. Leading foreign banks could acquire majority stakes in the Romanian banks slated for selloff, he added.
A long-awaited bank privatisation bill, a central part of previous loan accords with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, failed to clear parliament twice in 1996.
The former ruling leftists also failed to fulfil loan pledges to privatise two of the country's six state-run banks in 1995.

Development bank Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare SA and farm lender Banca Agricola SA are seen as the most likely candidates to turn private when the new centrist-dominated parliament resumes debates on the issue later this month.
The banking sector, which has now 40 commercial banks, was one of the fastest growing industries in post-communist Romania.
But the country's fledgling financial markets have been buffeted in recent years by scandals at two private banks and upsets in the investment fund industry.

Last July, Romania's central bank (BNR) cut support to Dacia Felix SA and Renasterea Creditului Romanesc Credit Bank SA, which revealed huge bad debts and losses. Courts have yet to rule on their fate -- liquidation or reorganisation.
BNR governor Mugur Isarescu said recently that his bank planned tougher rules on banking supervision and winding-up.
"We need tougher banking laws, with severe sanctions with special procedures for receivership and surveillance," he said.
"We also need a law to allow us quicker intervention," said Isarescu in a reference to present lengthy court procedures to decide on the fate of troubled banks.
Romanian banks can go into receivership only under a post-communist corporate law, which allows courts to delay their rulings for years.
